tier_reason: The repo README has no numbers; the numbers live in the SIGMOD'23 paper it links (cs.cit.tum.de vmcache.pdf), and every copy of that paper (TUM, osg.tuhh.de, ibr.cs.tu-bs.de, dl.acm.org) is egress-blocked here. A search snippet says WiredTiger and the mmap-based LMDB are significantly slower than vmcache and LeanStore, and that exmap is needed to reach full speed on fast storage. The paper is peer-reviewed, so this could become B once someone opens it; it stays C because the figures are snippet-only.

corrections.claimed_speedup: SIGMOD'23 paper (snippet only, PDF not opened): vmcache with exmap beats the mmap-based LMDB and WiredTiger on TPC-C and random-read workloads, and exmap is required to scale to high IOPS. The record's 'up to 67% and 35% read/s' figures could not be confirmed.
corrections.caveats: Numbers come from search snippets only, because the paper PDF host is egress-blocked; the record's 67%/35% exmap figures are unconfirmed. The comparison is against mmap-based systems (LMDB) and other buffer managers, not against a bare mmap loop. The repo README has the benchmark driver (TPC-C and random read via env vars) but no results. exmap (tuhhosg/exmap) is a separate Linux kernel module with no LICENSE file; module/driver.c declares MODULE_LICENSE("GPL"). vmcache itself is MIT and runs without exmap (EXMAP=0).

notes: Metadata checked on github.com: MIT, 86 stars, not a fork, last commit 2025-09-09 (active). Opening the paper (SIGMOD'23, DOI 10.1145/3588687) would allow a retier to B.

tier_reason: The README table compares wcp against cp -r and rsync on the author's machine, and the record's numbers match it exactly. The numbers are first-party; there is no benchmark script, and the CPU, compiler and flags are not stated (the build uses CMake Release).

corrections.claimed_speedup: 20x512MiB: wcp 3.97s (2579.59 MiB/s) vs cp -r 8.44s (1213.38 MiB/s); 7000x1MiB: 2.64s vs 8.29s; 200000x1KiB: 3.92s vs 9.23s (rsync 8.09s). The README headline says 'up to 70% faster than cp', which understates its own table (about 2.1-3.1x, derived from page data).
corrections.caveats: First-party numbers with no benchmark script; CPU and compiler not stated. Linux-only, using io_uring on kernel 5.6 or later. The author says it is probably not robust enough for daily use. Last commit 2021-05-21.

notes: Metadata checked on github.com: MIT, 222 stars, not a fork, last commit 2021-05-21, so abandoned is correct. The README file is readme.md in lowercase.

tier_reason: The README variant table (make benchvar) has std::cin 565 ms vs fio_mmap 66.5 ms and std::cout 473 ms vs fio_fread 148 ms; it states g++ 14.2 -O2 and the benchmark code is in the repo's src/ and Makefile. The CPU is given only as a 2-core Intel Xeon @2.60 GHz with no model, and the numbers are first-party, so the tier is C.

corrections.claimed_speedup: make benchvar: read 100 MiB std::cin 565 ms vs mmap + 2-byte table 66.5 ms (8.5x), main library fastio.hpp 70.7 ms (8.0x); write std::cout 473 ms vs fwrite + 4-digit table 148 ms (3.2x), main library 155 ms (3.05x). The README header says 69 ms (7.4x cin) read and 132 ms (3.25x cout) write. The make benchlib table gives cin/ifstream 489.6 ms vs 66.5 ms (7.4x) and cout/ofstream 469.5 ms vs 94.3 ms (5.0x).
corrections.caveats: The workload is integer parsing and formatting, so most of the gain is parsing rather than file I/O. The baseline is cin/cout with default sync; cin with sync off is about equal (578 ms). The README's headline numbers differ between its benchvar, benchlib and bench tables. The CPU model is not stated (2-core Xeon @2.60 GHz, 1.9 GiB RAM). __int128 support is a GNU extension. Repro commands: make benchvar, make benchlib and make bench.
